questions.q: 10,000 customers poll their order status every 5 seconds. Why is that a poor design?
questions.explain: Polling costs grow with the number of watchers times the polling rate, not with the number of changes. Pushing costs one message per change per watcher.
options: Browsers limit pages to one fetch per second
The server answers about 2,000 requests a second, nearly all saying "nothing changed", and customers still see changes up to 5 seconds late
Polling cannot send cookies
Polling only works over HTTP/2

questions.q: What is the main difference between Server-Sent Events and WebSockets?
questions.explain: With SSE, the client talks back with ordinary requests if it needs to. WebSockets are a separate protocol after the upgrade, suited to frequent two-way traffic.
options: SSE is encrypted, WebSockets are not
SSE sends events from server to client over one long HTTP response; WebSockets carry messages in both directions over an upgraded connection
WebSockets only work in Node.js
SSE can only send one event per connection

questions.q: What is the Last-Event-ID header for?
questions.explain: Every event with an id: updates the browser's last event id. On reconnect, the header lets the server resume instead of losing or repeating events, but only if the server honours it.
options: The server uses it to name the next event
When EventSource reconnects, it sends the id of the last event it received, so the server can send only what was missed
It tells the browser to stop reconnecting
It is a security token for the stream

questions.q: An order has been delivered and the page no longer needs its EventSource. The server ends the stream. What happens if the page does nothing?
questions.explain: An ended stream looks like a dropped connection, so EventSource reconnects. Only close() stops it (or a server answer with an error status or a wrong content type).
options: The EventSource closes for good
The browser reconnects after the retry delay, again and again; the page must call source.close()
The page reloads
An exception is thrown

questions.q: Why does the SSE server write : keep-alive every 15 seconds?
questions.explain: Idle connections are often closed after about a minute by infrastructure between the server and the browser. A small comment costs almost nothing and keeps the stream alive.
options: It is an event the page must handle
A line starting with : is a comment the browser ignores; sending it keeps proxies and load balancers from closing a quiet connection, and reveals dead connections to the server
It tells the browser the retry delay
It resets the event ids

questions.q: Why must a WebSocket server check the Origin header during the upgrade?
questions.explain: Without the check, a malicious page can open a socket as the logged-in user and read and send messages: cross-site WebSocket hijacking. Compare the origin against an exact allow-list.
options: Because the browser blocks WebSockets without it
WebSockets are not protected by CORS: any site can open one to your server with the user's cookies, and the Origin header is how the server knows which site is asking
Because ws:// URLs cannot contain paths
It is only needed for binary messages

questions.q: How does a WebSocket connection start?
questions.explain: Starting as HTTP lets WebSockets use the same ports, TLS and proxies as the web, and lets the server check cookies and the origin before agreeing.
options: With a UDP packet to port 80
With an HTTP request carrying Upgrade: websocket, answered by 101 Switching Protocols; the same connection then carries WebSocket frames
With an OPTIONS preflight
With a POST that the server never answers

questions.q: A chat page uses a WebSocket. The user's train goes through a tunnel for 20 seconds. What must the page's code do?
questions.explain: Unlike EventSource, a browser WebSocket never reconnects by itself and has no message history. Reconnection and catching up are the application's job.
options: Nothing; WebSocket reconnects and replays missed messages automatically
Notice the close event, reconnect with increasing delays, and then fetch the messages it missed, because nothing replays them
Reload the page
Switch to mode: "no-cors"

questions.q: A server sends a courier's location 50 times a second to a customer on a slow mobile network. What does socket.bufferedAmount tell the sender?
questions.explain: send never blocks, so a fast sender and a slow network fill memory. For location updates, only the newest one matters, so dropping old ones is correct.
options: How many messages the customer has read
How many bytes are queued and not yet sent; if it keeps growing, the sender should slow down or drop stale updates
The maximum message size
The network's speed in bytes per second

questions.q: Why do WebSocket servers send a ping every 30 seconds or so?
questions.explain: TCP can take a very long time to notice a peer that disappeared. Pings detect it quickly, and they also keep idle-timeout proxies from closing healthy connections.
options: To measure the user's typing speed
A client that vanished (lost signal, closed laptop) sends no close message; a missing pong reveals the dead connection so the server can clean it up
Because messages expire after 30 seconds
To keep the TLS certificate valid

questions.q: The courier chat runs on two server processes behind a load balancer. The customer is connected to process A and the courier to process B. Their messages never arrive. Why, and what fixes it?
questions.explain: In-memory rooms work on one process only. With several, each process publishes messages to a shared bus and delivers what it receives to its local sockets.
options: WebSockets cannot pass through load balancers
Each process only knows its own sockets, so rooms are split; a shared pub/sub channel (such as Redis) lets every process deliver every room's messages
The two processes need different ports
The courier must reconnect every second

questions.q: A site uses HTTP/1.1 and one EventSource per tab. A user opens seven tabs, and the seventh never loads its data. Why?
questions.explain: Long-lived streams hold connections. Serve them over HTTP/2, or share one stream between tabs (with a SharedWorker or a BroadcastChannel).
options: Servers refuse more than six streams per user
Browsers allow about six HTTP/1.1 connections per host, and each open event stream keeps one busy; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection
EventSource only works in one tab at a time
The seventh tab has no cookies

questions.q: The event stream works on a developer's machine but in production the page receives nothing for a minute, then everything at once. What is the usual cause?
questions.explain: SSE depends on each event being passed on immediately. Buffering reverse proxies (and gzip middleware) hold data back; nginx, for example, respects an X-Accel-Buffering: no header.
options: The server's clock is wrong
A proxy or compression layer buffers the response before passing it on; turn buffering and compression off for the stream
The browser caches event streams
Production needs ws:// instead of http://

questions.q: A page runs worker.postMessage(order) and on the next line order.status = "cancelled". Which status does the worker see?
questions.explain: Structured clone copies the data when postMessage is called. Later changes on either side affect only that side's copy.
options: "cancelled", because objects are shared between threads
The status at the moment of postMessage, because the message is copied when it is sent
Whichever change happens last
undefined, because objects cannot be posted

questions.q: What happens to an ArrayBuffer listed as a transferable in worker.postMessage({ photo }, [photo])?
questions.explain: Transferring avoids copying large data, at the cost of the sender losing access. Sharing memory between threads needs SharedArrayBuffer, which has extra security requirements.
options: It is copied, and both sides keep a copy
Ownership moves to the worker without copying; the page's buffer becomes empty (byteLength 0)
It is shared, and both sides see each other's changes
It is compressed

questions.q: Code in a worker throws an uncaught exception. What does the page's try { await callWorker(…) } catch see?
questions.explain: The worker runs on another thread with its own call stack. Catch errors inside the worker and send them back in a reply, as the lesson's wrapper did, and give calls a timeout.
options: The exception, as a rejection
Nothing: the error fires an error event on the Worker object, and the waiting promise never settles unless the code handles it
A DataCloneError
The page reloads

questions.q: Which pairing of feature and tool is best?
questions.explain: Pick by direction and frequency: one-way news fits SSE, two-way chat fits WebSockets, heavy local work fits a worker, and something that happens once a day fits a simple poll or a notification.
options: Delivery driver chat: polling every 30 seconds
Parsing a 50 MB bank statement in the page: WebSocket
Order status updates: Server-Sent Events; courier chat: WebSocket; parsing a large file: Web Worker
Nightly report ready: WebSocket kept open all day

questions.q: What should a WebSocket server do with each incoming message?
questions.explain: A socket message is like a request body from a stranger. The lesson's server refused a location from a customer and text that was not JSON, and forwarded only fields it had checked.
options: Broadcast it unchanged to the room; clients will validate it
Treat it as untrusted input: parse it safely, check its type, fields, size and whether this user may send it, then build a new message to forward
Evaluate it as JavaScript
Insert it into the other clients' pages with innerHTML

questions.q: Why does each status event carry the whole new status ({"status":"packed"}) rather than an instruction like "advance one step"?
questions.explain: Events that describe the resulting state are idempotent. Combined with ignoring ids that were already applied, the page stays correct whatever the network does.
options: It makes events smaller
Applying the same event twice then does no harm, so replays and duplicates after reconnecting cannot push the order past its real status
Browsers cannot parse instructions
So that events need no ids

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Printing the string through JSON.stringify shows its line breaks as \n and escapes the inner quotes. The event ends with a blank line (two \n). Stringifying the data keeps it on one data: line.
options:
"id: 3
event: status
data: {"status":"packed"}

"

"id: 3
event: status
data: [object Object]

"
"id: 3 event: status data: {"status":"packed"}"
{"id":3,"event":"status","data":{"status":"packed"}}

questions.q: A server keeps event ids as strings and resumes from Last-Event-ID. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two strings are compared character by character: "10" > "9" is false because "1" comes before "9". Headers are always strings, so convert ids to numbers before comparing, or the client silently misses every event after id 9.

questions.q: After reconnects, events arrive with these ids. What does this print?
questions.explain: Duplicates and anything older than the last applied id are skipped. Event 4 arrived after 5 and is dropped too, which is right for "latest status" feeds; a feed where every event matters would instead need to fill the gap.

questions.q: MessageChannel passes messages the same way as a worker. What does this print?
questions.explain: Messages are delivered asynchronously, so the synchronous log comes first. The message was copied when it was posted, so the receiver sees paid, in an object that is not the original.
options:
sent, then changed to: delivered
received: paid false

received: paid false
sent, then changed to: delivered

sent, then changed to: delivered
received: delivered true

sent, then changed to: delivered
received: delivered false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Transferring moves the memory: the original buffer is detached and reports length 0. A normal clone copies, and both keep their data. postMessage(data, [buffer]) behaves the same way.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: readyState moves from 0 (connecting) to 1 (open), then 2 (closing) and 3 (closed). Only send while it is 1. EventSource uses 0, 1 and 2 for connecting, open and closed.
options: connecting open closing closed

questions.explain: A broadcast goes to everyone in the room except the sender. An unknown room gives an empty list thanks to ?? [], instead of crashing the server.

questions.explain: "null" is valid JSON, so parsing succeeds and message is null; optional chaining (?.) keeps the checks from throwing. The long chat message breaks the 20-character limit, and customers may not send locations.

questions.q: Replies arrive in a different order from the calls. What does this print?
questions.explain: The id in each reply finds the right waiting promise, whatever order the replies come in. Deleting the entry after use keeps the map from growing forever.
options:
totalKobo -> 1930000
slowest -> ORD-1042 0

totalKobo -> ORD-1042
slowest -> 1930000 0

slowest -> ORD-1042
totalKobo -> 1930000 0

totalKobo -> 1930000

questions.q: Write formatEvent({ id, event, data }) that returns the text of one SSE event. Include id: and event: lines only when given. data is a string that may contain line breaks: write one data: line per line of it. End with a blank line.
questions.explain: A raw line break inside data would end the field early, and a blank line would end the event. Splitting into several data: lines is how the format carries multi-line text; the browser joins them again.
questions.expected:
"id: 4
event: status
data: {"status":"delivered"}

"
"data: Your rider is Musa.
data: He will call on arrival.

"

questions.q: Network chunks can end in the middle of an event. Write splitEvents(buffer) that returns { blocks, rest }: every complete event block (text before a "\n\n") in order, and the unfinished text left over for the next chunk.
questions.explain: The first chunk held no complete event, so everything was kept for later. A parser that assumed one chunk equals one event would have produced "pa" and then garbage. This buffer is the heart of every stream parser, including readEvents in the lesson.

questions.q: Write createDeduper() returning accept(id). It converts id to a number and returns true (and remembers it) only if it is larger than every id accepted so far. Ids that are not whole numbers return false.
questions.explain: Converting first avoids the string comparison trap ("10" < "9"). The closure keeps the last accepted id, the same state EventSource keeps as lastEventId.
questions.expected: true true false true false false true

questions.q: Write reconnectDelay(attempt, random): the base delay is 500 ms for attempt 1 and doubles each attempt, capped at 30,000 ms; the result is Math.round(base / 2 + random() * (base / 2)).
questions.explain: With random fixed at 0.5, each delay is three quarters of its base. The cap stops the delay growing forever, and in real use the random part spreads thousands of reconnecting clients over time.

questions.q: Write createClient(port) for a worker-style port (an object with postMessage and an onmessage property). call(method, args) sends { id, method, args } and returns a promise that resolves with the reply's result, or rejects with new Error(reply.error).
questions.explain: The refund's error arrived first, but each reply found its own promise by id. The .catch is attached straight away: a rejection nobody is listening for yet counts as unhandled, and Node.js stops the program for it. The fake port lets you test the client without a real worker; the same code works with new Worker(…).

questions.q: Write createRooms() with join(room, member), leave(room, member) and broadcast(room, sender, text). broadcast returns the list of "member: text" deliveries to everyone in the room except the sender. An empty room must be deleted when its last member leaves (report the number of rooms with count()).
questions.explain: Deleting empty rooms matters on a long-running server: every finished order would otherwise leave an empty Set in memory forever. That is the same clean-up the lesson's server does in its close handler.

questions.q: An API authenticates every request with an Authorization: Bearer … header. Why is EventSource awkward for it?
questions.explain: The browser's EventSource constructor takes only a URL and a credentials flag. Putting a token in the URL leaks it into logs, so prefer an HttpOnly session cookie, or read the stream with fetch, which can set headers, as the lesson's Node.js client did.
options: EventSource cannot use HTTPS
EventSource cannot set custom request headers; it can only send cookies (with withCredentials across origins), so the feed needs cookie authentication or a fetch-based stream reader
EventSource strips the cookie header
Bearer tokens only work with WebSockets

questions.explain: Three updates before the first frame schedule only one frame, which renders the latest value, 3. After it runs, the next update schedules a new frame. Only two frames were ever requested.

questions.q: A slow connection can only hold two queued location updates, so the oldest is dropped. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each new update pushes out the oldest once the queue is full, so only the two newest remain. For live locations that is exactly right: a stale position has no value, and memory stays bounded however slow the network is.

questions.q: A worker call that never gets a reply leaves a promise pending forever. Write withTimeout(promise, ms) that resolves like promise, or rejects with new Error("no reply after <ms> ms") if it takes longer. Clear the timer when the promise wins.
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first. Clearing the timer in finally means a fast reply does not leave a timer running for nothing. A worker wrapper would also delete the call from its pending map on timeout.
